entities.summary: Menecrates of Syracuse, Magna Graecia, was the physician at the court of Philip of Macedon, 359–336 BC. He seems to have been a successful practitioner, but to have made himself ridiculous by calling himself Zeus, and assuming divine honors. He would give the names of various gods to those he successfully treated. He once wrote a letter to Philip, beginning :Zeus-Menecrates to Philip, greeting: You are king of Macedonia, but I am king of Medicine. You can destroy healthy people whensoever you wish, but I can save the ailing, and the robust who follow my prescriptions I can keep alive without sickness until old age comes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Menecrates' boasts about his medical abilities and divine honors may have been seen as hubris by some, but they also demonstrate the growing influence of Greek medicine in the ancient world. His claims highlight the importance of physicians like Menecrates in shaping the medical practices of their time.
